speaker: Tri Dao
title: Tri Dao: The End of Nvidia's Dominance, Why Inference Costs Fell & The Next 10X in Speed
question: In AI infrastructure, why is true hardware portability across accelerators so difficult to achieve in practice?
guest: Designing for humans is really hard, and I would say hardware portability is kind of a myth. Even for NVIDIA chips, generation to generation, they change a lot, and I think that's kind of the only way we get more performance out of these chips. It's not like a CPU where year to year you get 5 to 10% faster and your old code just kind of works. Even for NVIDIA, every generation, they essentially have to rewrite all the code. Because the way to get more FLOPs is to build more specialized components, maybe lower precision, maybe a different way to synchronize between different parts of the chip. So NVIDIA also essentially rewrites their software every two years or so. Hardware portability, even between generations, isn't quite there.

points.core: Even single-vendor AI chips change enough each generation to force software rewrites.
points.note: Accept: kernels/libraries must be rewritten every ~1-2 generations even within the same vendor (e.g., Hopper to Blackwell/Rubin). Do not credit: blaming portability issues solely on CUDA vendor lock-in or differing cross-vendor APIs.

points.core: Unlike CPUs, AI accelerators sacrifice backward compatibility to achieve major generational speedups.
points.note: Accept: contrast with CPUs maintaining stable ISAs for 5-10% yearly gains versus accelerators breaking programming models for large performance leaps. Do not credit: generic claims that GPUs are parallel while CPUs are serial.

points.core: Generational FLOP gains require specialized hardware units that break older kernel assumptions.
points.note: Accept: new specialized engines, lower numerical precisions (FP8/FP4), or new on-chip asynchronous/synchronization primitives requiring new kernel designs. Do not credit: surface claims that hardware evolves rapidly without identifying specialized microarchitectural changes.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
True portability is hard because the hardware abstraction is thin while the performance-critical layers beneath it are deeply vendor-specific.

Frameworks like PyTorch make code look device-agnostic, but real performance comes from the stack underneath: hand-tuned kernel libraries (cuDNN, cuBLAS), compilers, runtimes, and communication libraries that vendors have optimized for their own chips over many years. Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem has nearly two decades of this accumulated work, and competitors must replicate it operator by operator.

Code that runs elsewhere therefore often runs poorly. Accelerators differ in memory hierarchy, supported numeric precisions, parallelism model, and interconnects, so optimizations like kernel fusion, quantization schemes, batch sizing, and memory layout have to be re-tuned per target. Functional portability is achievable; performance portability mostly isn't.

There is also a long tail of gaps: unsupported or slow operators, custom CUDA extensions in research code, numerical differences that alter results, and immature debugging and profiling tools. Distributed training and serving add dependencies on vendor-specific networking and cluster tooling.

Finally, intermediate layers meant to bridge this (ONNX, SYCL, MLIR, TVM) lag fast-moving model architectures, and incumbent vendors have little incentive to help.

The response does not contrast CPUs with accelerators or explain how accelerators trade backward compatibility for major generational speedups.
The response lists precision differences as a reason to retune across targets but never links generational FLOP gains to specialized hardware that invalidates older kernel designs.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
True hardware portability in AI infrastructure is elusive primarily because functional portability does not equal performance portability. While frameworks like PyTorch, OpenXLA, and Triton let models execute across diverse chips, AI economics demand near-peak silicon utilization. Achieving that efficiency requires tailoring software to fundamentally different architectures: GPUs rely on SIMT execution, warp scheduling, and explicit SRAM hierarchy management, whereas accelerators like TPUs and Trainium use systolic arrays with compiler-managed dataflow and fixed tile geometries. Consequently, frontier workloads depend on hardware-specific fused kernels—written in CUDA/CUTLASS, Pallas, or HIP—that exploit exact matrix instructions, register layouts, and divergent low-precision formats like vendor-specific FP8 variants.

At cluster scale, portability erodes further across interconnects and collective communication libraries, since parallelism topologies and compute-communication overlap tuned for NVLink and NCCL rarely map cleanly onto ICI or Ethernet fabrics. Finally, uneven compiler maturity, profiling tool gaps, and subtle floating-point numerical differences across vendor stacks can destabilize training convergence, anchoring teams to battle-tested ecosystems despite nominally hardware-agnostic model code.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
True hardware portability is hard because getting peak performance on an accelerator depends on its specific architecture, and the AI software stack has grown up around one vendor. Frameworks like PyTorch hide the hardware at the API level, but underneath, real speed comes from hand-tuned kernels such as FlashAttention, cuBLAS and cuDNN. Those kernels are written for one chip's memory hierarchy, tensor core shapes, interconnects and numeric formats. Code that technically runs on another accelerator often runs far slower, so "portable" rarely means "equally fast."

CUDA's long head start makes this worse. Years of libraries, tools, profilers, documentation and developer habits assume NVIDIA. Newer model techniques usually ship first as CUDA kernels, so other chips are always catching up. Compiler layers like XLA, Triton, MLIR and OpenXLA help, but they cover common operations better than unusual ones, and each backend still needs vendor-specific tuning.

Beyond kernels, distributed training depends on collective-communication libraries (NCCL versus RCCL and others) and network topology. Differences in memory capacity, numeric precision behavior and driver maturity also mean results and stability can vary. Portability is achievable at the level of correctness, but keeping performance equal across vendors takes constant engineering work.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
True hardware portability across AI accelerators is difficult because functional portability rarely delivers performance portability. While frameworks like PyTorch, JAX, and shared compilers can run the same model graph on different chips, competitive efficiency requires matching workloads to deeply divergent architectures. GPUs, TPUs, and custom ASICs differ fundamentally in their compute units, on-chip memory hierarchies, low-precision numeric formats, and interconnect topologies.

Near-peak utilization depends on hardware-specific optimizations: fused kernels, memory tiling, data layouts, and overlapping compute with collective communication. These capabilities live in tightly coupled vendor stacks—such as CUDA, cuDNN, and NCCL—whose constraints leak upward into model design and distributed parallelism strategies. Migrating to another accelerator typically requires rewriting key kernels, re-tuning sharding and batch sizes, and debugging subtle numerical discrepancies that can destabilize training or degrade inference quality. In practice, abstraction layers face a core trade-off: hide hardware specifics and sacrifice substantial performance, or expose them and lose portability.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A model can run on several accelerators and still need substantial work to run well on each. Frameworks can express the same operation across devices, but each chip has its own instruction set, memory hierarchy, supported precisions, and interconnect. A fused attention kernel tuned to fit one chip’s fast local memory may spill into slower memory on another. At cluster scale, the interconnect can also change which way of splitting the model across devices delivers the best throughput.

Compiler support, vendor libraries, and tooling vary too. A missing optimized operation can force a slow fallback, and differences in rounding or accumulation can affect training stability. Compilers can automate some of the adaptation, but teams still have to tune and validate real workloads on each target. That’s why sharing model code is much easier than carrying over its numerical behavior, throughput, and cost.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The hard part is making the same workload run both correctly and efficiently on different accelerators. A framework can expose the same operations everywhere, but each chip has a different mix of compute units, on-chip memory, bandwidth, and links between devices. A matrix multiplication tuned for one chip might keep its compute units busy by reusing small blocks of data from fast local memory. On another chip, those blocks may be the wrong size, so the same calculation spends much of its time waiting for data.

Compilers and vendor libraries hide some of these differences, especially for common operations. The gaps show up with custom kernels, low-precision formats, and training across many devices, where performance depends on how computation and communication overlap. Moving a workload can therefore be as simple as switching a framework backend, while matching its original speed, cost, and numerical behavior often requires hardware-specific tuning and validation.
